questions.question: When planning pretraining compute, which two quantities does the lesson identify as the main allocation knobs?
options: Inference prompts and output temperature
Model parameters and training tokens
Batch size and sequence vocabulary
GPU count and attention head count
questions.explanation: The lesson models training compute mainly through parameter count N and token count D, with approximate cost C ≈ 6ND. A larger GPU count is an implementation resource, not one of the two quantities allocated inside that scaling relation.

questions.question: Under the approximation C ≈ 6ND, what compute budget trains N=1 billion parameters on D=20 billion tokens?
options: 1.2 × 10²¹ FLOPs
2.0 × 10¹⁹ FLOPs
1.2 × 10¹⁹ FLOPs
1.2 × 10²⁰ FLOPs
questions.explanation: Substitute the values into C ≈ 6ND: 6 × 10⁹ parameters × 20 × 10⁹ tokens = 120 × 10¹⁸ = 1.2 × 10²⁰ FLOPs. Omitting the coefficient six understates the budget sixfold.

questions.question: At a fixed compute budget C = 6ND, what happens to the allowed token count if parameter count doubles?
options: The token count grows by a factor of four
The token count stays unchanged
The token count is cut in half
The token count doubles as well
questions.explanation: With C fixed, solve for tokens: D = C/(6N). Doubling N therefore halves the available D; doubling both N and D would instead quadruple compute and break the fixed-budget condition.

questions.question: Why might an inference-heavy product train a smaller model on more tokens than the compute-optimal split?
options: A smaller model reduces inference cost paid repeatedly
A larger model always needs fewer training tokens
More tokens remove the model’s parameter memory
The training compute is charged on every inference request
questions.explanation: When serving dominates lifetime cost, reducing parameter count lowers the compute paid on every inference request, while training cost is paid once. The product can spend more pretraining compute for a smaller deployable model; training is not charged again per request.

questions.question: An 8B model sees 15 trillion training tokens. What is its token-to-parameter ratio?
options: 1,875 tokens per parameter
20 tokens per parameter
187.5 tokens per parameter
15 tokens per parameter
questions.explanation: The ratio is D/N = 15×10¹² ÷ 8×10⁹ = 1,875 tokens per parameter. The 20-token value is the described compute-optimal reference, while this model’s data-to-size ratio is much larger.

questions.question: A benchmark shows a sudden score jump, while validation cross-entropy improves smoothly. How should the team interpret it?
options: The cross-entropy is unusable for scaling comparisons
The model necessarily learned a new discrete capability
The evaluation set must contain no difficult examples
The benchmark threshold may hide smooth underlying gains
questions.explanation: A thresholded benchmark can convert gradually improving logits into a sudden change in accuracy once examples cross the scoring cutoff. Smooth cross-entropy reveals that underlying trend, so the score jump alone does not prove a newly discrete ability.
